Michael R Douglas said:

  • plus a closure-status axis (discharged / declared-on-closure / declared-off-closure) so "every headline is axiom-clean" and "N axioms still declared" never get conflated

I'm very skeptical about mixing in any analysis of axioms or sorries into such a system. Anything that has axioms or sorries is a private, in-progress project, and not ready for anyone to be thinking about whether its correct or not: it's just wrong if it has an axiom or sorry, and we shouldn't even bother turning Lean on.

It's fine to write def MyHypothesis : Prop := ... and then theorem myConditionalTheorem (p : MyHypothesis) : ... := ..., and that avoids the need for sorry or axiom, and you can do all the human assurance / vetting at the MyHypothesis level.
I like the general ideas here, but it seems like it has a lot of moving pieces that are tightly coupled. Who keeps the prose companions in sync with the Lean-checked material?
3 messages were moved here from #Tau Ceti > Possible next steps by Kim Morrison.
Of course Tau Ceti does not have to accept projects with axioms or sorry, this is a general framework which supports them in the development process.

Yes, but I'm saying that your framework is weaker (i.e. less convincing, and thus less useful), because of that additional flexibility to support axioms or sorry.

I know my attitude towards axiom and sorry is not univerally shared, but I think it's the hard won lesson of years of building trust in Lean projects. :woman_shrugging:
It's OK for one community, but other communities will find axioms (and maybe sorry) useful. A lot of physics could be formalized if we admit well chosen axioms.

I like the general ideas here, but it seems like it has a lot of moving pieces that are tightly coupled. Who keeps the prose companions in sync with the Lean-checked material?

It's work, like keeping docstrings current or making blueprints. Work which the human readers and reviewers will appreciate. I am putting the focus on the important questions: how do we convince humans that a formalization is correct? How do we help humans learn from it?

Michael R Douglas said:

if we admit well chosen axioms.

@Michael R Douglas, could you explain what axioms gain over just defining something as a Prop, as I sketch above? It lets you do everything that axiom lets you do, without allowing unconditional proofs of False when you get something wrong.

The two options are semantically similar, yes. But suppose I introduce a new axiom, I have to carry it around explicitly into everything that uses it. Which has advantages and disadvantages. If it's an axiom which is beyond doubt, say it's a well established theorem but not yet formalized, or one of the standard postulates in a physics argument, then mostly disadvantages. Maybe there is a syntactic way to deal with this. Separately from that, people regularly use sorry and axiom in the course of developing a project, and I set up this framework to help in development and then be useful when the project is done.

Kim Morrison said:

Michael R Douglas, could you explain what axioms gain over just defining something as a Prop, as I sketch above? It lets you do everything that axiom lets you do, without allowing unconditional proofs of False when you get something wrong.

It won't be unconditional, right? It still shows up in #print axioms.
If someone shows me a proof of False, and I see uncontroversialPhysicsPostulate in the output of #print axioms, then....
You'll shrug and say "could you please not post repositories with axiom?" :-)

Whereas if there are 10 repos with 80KLOC each that have statements of the form

theorem FooBar (h : uncontroversialPhysicsPostulate) : cool Result := blah

and then someone comes along with

example (h : uncontroversialPhysicsPostulate) : False := mwah

then...
4 messages were moved here from #Tau Ceti > Auditing definitions by Johan Commelin.

I think one benefit of conditional results over axioms is that you can prove that certain conditions imply each other. Whereas you can't clean up the amount of axioms that you depend on by showing that some imply others.

What about results that depend on some complicated numerical calculation, this for example happens in some modularity proofs where you need to compute something on a modular curve. Here I would think that since we are unlikely to want to redo this calculation in lean, it would make sense to have it as an axiom instead of passing around an extra hypothesis in all of your results.
Right, that’s a good example of an axiom which is beyond doubt. I would agree though that sometimes conditional results are the right tool. Both should be available.

In Physlib we get around this problem with the @[sorryful] attribute - the idea being that anything that depends on the Sorry axiom (even transitively) must be tagged by this attribute (enforced by a linter). This makes it visually easy to see which results can be totally trusted and which can be trusted only up-to some results which are included with a sorry without having to run something like #print axioms ... every-time or carry around hypothesis. Could naturally be extended to different axioms. (Though this is likely not to everyones taste)
